title: The Inflammation Theory of Disease
summary: Josh and Chuck (with iHeart Intro segments) explain the inflammation theory of disease: the difference between acute inflammation (a healthy immune defense with redness, swelling, heat, pain, impaired function) and chronic systemic inflammation, which may underlie many noncommunicable diseases. Topics include causes of chronic inflammation (persistent infections, oxidative stress/free radicals, autoimmune disorders), links to Alzheimer's disease and neuroinflammation, depression and sickness behaviors, lung and colon cancer, the role of industrialization, diet, microplastics and chemicals, sedentary lifestyle, stress, shift work, aging, and the CRP blood test. The episode also includes a brief announcement about the updated website, and a listener mail segment from Kaya Powell.

segments.title: Opening banter and studio move
segments.summary: Hosts banter about Chuck's move to a new home studio, Governor's awards, and a segue into inflammation.

segments.title: What inflammation is and its Latin roots
segments.summary: The word inflammation comes from Latin flammatio, and Galen's four classic signs (redness, swelling, heat, pain) plus impaired function are introduced.

segments.title: Acute inflammation and the immune response
segments.summary: Acute inflammation is a healthy defense: immune cells release mediators like histamine and bradykinin that dilate blood vessels and cause pain and fluid buildup.

segments.title: Swollen lymph nodes and personal anecdote
segments.summary: Swollen lymph nodes and runny noses are explained as inflammatory processes; Chuck recalls a swollen node after a hospital visit.

segments.title: From acute to chronic inflammation
segments.summary: Inflammation becomes harmful when it persists long after it should stop, which is the basis of the unifying theory of disease.

segments.title: Causes: persistent infections, oxidative stress, autoimmunity
segments.summary: Chronic inflammation can be triggered by persistent infections such as hepatitis, HIV, and possibly long COVID; by oxidative stress from free radicals; and by autoimmune disorders like lupus.

segments.title: Diseases linked to chronic inflammation
segments.summary: A list of major killers linked to chronic inflammation: high blood pressure, heart disease, type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease, IBS, inflammatory bowel disease, asthma, some cancers, rheumatoid arthritis, depression, Parkinson's, dementia, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.

segments.title: Cause or symptom debate
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether chronic inflammation causes these diseases or is a symptom, with Josh arguing it is the cause, using sugar as an example.

segments.title: Alzheimer's disease and neuroinflammation
segments.summary: Alzheimer's is reviewed as amyloid plaques and tau tangles, then neuroinflammation is presented as a possible root cause; microglia may attack healthy neurons. Autopsy studies are cited on both sides.

segments.title: Potential impact of solving chronic inflammation
segments.summary: The hosts discuss that about half of annual deaths (67 million in 2022) are linked to chronic inflammation, and the potential effect on population and quality of life.

segments.title: Economic cost of chronic inflammation
segments.summary: In 2016 the US spent about 1.1 trillion dollars directly on healthcare for chronic inflammation-related diseases, and about 3.7 trillion including lost productivity.

segments.title: Smoking, lung cancer and colon cancer
segments.summary: Smoke irritates lung cells, causing inflammation and reactive oxygen species that damage DNA and can lead to tumors. Crohn's and ulcerative colitis raise colon cancer risk. Chronic infections like HPV and tuberculosis are also linked to cancer via inflammation.

segments.title: Depression and inflammation
segments.summary: About a third of people with depression do not respond to SSRIs, suggesting neuroinflammation may cause depression for some. Autopsy studies and an interferon alpha study in cancer patients are cited.

segments.title: Sickness behaviors and evolutionary explanation
segments.summary: Sickness behaviors such as fatigue, anhedonia, and social withdrawal may have evolved to help the body rest while sick, and the brain may confuse them with depression.

segments.title: Evolutionary mismatch and uncontacted tribes
segments.summary: Modern chronic diseases may stem from an evolutionary mismatch with modern industrial life. Uncontacted tribes are noted as lacking type 2 diabetes and IBS, and the hosts reject aging alone as the explanation.

segments.title: Environmental toxins, microplastics and chemicals
segments.summary: Pollution, microplastics, and forever chemicals are discussed as sources of inflammation. Josh notes about 150,000 industrial chemicals with around 2,000 added yearly and limited FDA testing.

segments.title: Inflammatory diet and Mediterranean diet
segments.summary: Fried food, sugary sodas, refined sugar, trans fats, processed meats, and alcohol are inflammatory; the Mediterranean diet (olive oil, leafy greens, fish, berries, nuts) is anti-inflammatory. The Western diet is low in fiber.

segments.title: Exercise, sedentary lifestyle and belly fat
segments.summary: Contracting skeletal muscle releases anti-inflammatory proteins; half of American adults are not physically active. Visceral belly fat is also described as causing inflammation. Chuck mentions weight loss.

segments.title: Website announcement
segments.summary: Hosts announce the updated stuffyoushouldknow.com website with all episodes and improved search.

segments.title: Sleep, shift work, circadian rhythm and aging
segments.summary: Screens and shift work disrupt circadian rhythm, which promotes inflammation and raises risk of cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, obesity, and cancer. Immunosenescence with aging is also described.

segments.title: Testing for inflammation and lifestyle changes
segments.summary: The CRP blood test (hs-CRP) indicates chronic inflammation but not its location. Lifestyle changes like exercise, healthy weight, less processed food, quitting smoking, sleep, reducing alcohol, and social connection can help.

segments.title: Closing remarks on family and grandparents
segments.summary: Hosts close with personal reflections on grandparents and advice to talk with older relatives.

segments.title: Listener mail from Kaya Powell
segments.summary: Kaya Powell writes that she listened to the show with her dad on car trips starting around 2013, and now as a college student still listens.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Standard closing with iHeartRadio credit and mail address.
